{"path": "/home/bob/books/First_Generation/Chapter_05_Two_Year_Thinking.md", "content": "# Chapter 5 — Two-Year Thinking

*Mission AI: "Commander Vasquez, atmospheric pressure nominal at 612 pascals. External temperature minus sixty-two Celsius, rising marginally with dawn cycle. All habitat seals holding. Radiation environment within expected parameters. I have logged forty-seven hours since last confirmed reception from Houston Mission Control. I am continuing to cycle all telemetry buffers per standby protocol 9B."*

Elena sat in the communications alcove with the lights turned down to a warm amber that felt almost human in a room full of unforgiving hardware. The comms panel had been dark for three days now, and in those three days she had developed the habit of sitting here longer than necessary, as if proximity to the equipment could coax something back to life through force of will.

Behind her, the habitat slept in fragments — people shifting in narrow bunks, murmuring in languages that weren't English when they thought they were alone, dreaming about gravity.

*Mission AI: "I have detected a fluctuation in the water reclamation subsystem, Loop B. Efficiency has dropped to eighty-nine percent. I recommend inspection of the catalytic filter housing at your convenience."*

"I'll get to it," Elena said softly, though it wasn't a complaint and she wasn't annoyed. The AI was doing exactly what it had been designed to do: notice, report, log, wait. It was a competent employee and a terrible conversationalist. She appreciated both things about it.

Her hand rested on the comms console. The silence from Earth was wrong. Not the static kind of wrong — static was natural, expected, the background radiation of the universe saying hello. This was a different kind of silence. The kind that arrives because something on the other end has stopped speaking.

Three days. In Houston, someone would know why. Someone would be looking at the same gap in the signal, running diagnostics, calling engineers in the middle of their dinners, swearing at equipment that probably wasn't the problem.

But she couldn't know any of that from here, 225 million kilometers away, sitting in a pressurized tin can on a planet that wanted nothing to do with human visitors.

*Mission AI: "Scheduled briefing window opens in twelve minutes, Commander. The crew is assembled in the galley."*

Elena stood up, stretched her back against the low ceiling, and went to face her people.

---

The galley was the largest single room in the habitat, which was like calling a shoebox the most spacious container in a desk drawer. Six fold-out seats clustered around a central table that could be reconfigured into a work surface, a dining area, or — on days when someone needed the floor space — temporarily dismantled. Nobody wanted temporary right now. They wanted permanent. They wanted the floor to stay still.

Elena walked in to find her crew already settled. Arun Patel at the far end, his tablet propped open, dark circles under his eyes that had nothing to do with sleep and everything to do with the kind of thinking that never stopped. Imani Okoro beside him, her arms crossed in that particular way she had when she was preparing to disagree with something before it was even said. Chen Wei in the corner seat, quiet, attentive, a pen already moving across a physical notebook because some people still trusted paper more than silicon when things felt precarious. Tomas Eriksen closest to the door, always closest to the door, his posture relaxed but his eyes always checking, always scanning.

"Thank you for being on time," Elena said, not sure if she was being funny. Nobody laughed. They rarely laughed these days. "I called this briefing because I think we need to revisit some of the mission assumptions we've been operating under."

She pulled up a chair and sat at the head of the table. The screen on the wall behind her booted, showing the mission timeline they all knew by heart but needed to see again.

"We came to Mars on a two-year plan," Elena began. "That's not negotiable. It's not aspirational. It is — was — baked into every supply calculation, every ration package, every spare part we brought in the cargo modules. Two years on Mars, then we go home."

She tapped the screen. The timeline appeared, clean lines and colored bars, the kind of project management graphic that made complexity look manageable.

"Year one: establish habitat, deploy scientific instruments, begin baseline surveys. That's done." The first section of the bar was filled in solid green. "Year two: deep operations, extended EVAs, sample caching for return. We're entering that now." The second section was partially filled, halfway through. "And then —" she hesitated, just a fraction, enough that Chen noticed and stopped writing and Imani's arms shifted fractionally tighter "— then we board the ascent vehicle, rendezvous with the Earth Return Vehicle in Mars orbit, and we come home."

The final section of the bar was empty, outlined in white, waiting to be filled.

"The two-year timeline wasn't a suggestion from Mission Planning," Elena continued. "It was an engineering constraint. Our food stocks, calculated to the day with a fifteen percent safety margin, support two years and approximately one hundred days. Our suit rotation schedule is designed for that window. Spare parts, medical supplies, water reclamation filters — every single consumable was chosen to last two years with comfortable margin and nothing more. We were never intended to be here longer."

Arun had been staring at the timeline the whole time she spoke, and now he raised his head. His voice was calm, the voice he used when he was about to say something that might hurt.

"And if we're here longer?" he asked. Not rhetorically. He genuinely wanted her to answer.

Elena met his eyes. "Then we have a problem that we weren't supposed to have."

Silence settled over the room. Tomas shifted in his seat, the chair creaking. Chen closed his notebook slowly. Imani's expression changed — not to fear, exactly, but to the focused intensity of a scientist recalibrating her entire framework.

"The communication loss," Imani said. "You think it relates."

"I think the communication loss is the first thing that we can measure," Elena said. "Whatever's happening on Earth, we're not hearing about it. We don't know if it's temporary, technical, or something else. But the fact that it happened means we need to think about our timeline differently. Not with panic. With math. We have the data. We can run the calculations ourselves, even without Houston."

"We can stretch the rations," Chen said, speaking for the first time. His English was precise and economical, every word placed. "If we reconfigure caloric distribution now, reduce individual intake by eight to ten percent, combine with what the greenhouse modules produce — assuming they continue to yield — we could add perhaps six months."

"Six months is a lot," Tomas said, though his tone suggested he was trying to convince himself. "Six months is — we can fix things in six months. Comms should come back, and if they don't, we'll have time to think about alternatives."

"Alternatives," Arun said. He said it the way someone says a diagnosis.

Elena nodded. "We'll run the numbers. Each subsystem independently, then combined. Imani, you take environmental controls. Arun, power systems. Chen, consumables and food. Tomas, you coordinate EVA capability assessment — how many suit cycles we have left, what replacements are feasible. I want numbers, I want ranges, and I want worst-case scenarios. Not because the worst case is likely. Because we owe it to ourselves to know."

"What about the ERV?" Imani asked. The Earth Return Vehicle. The thing that would get them home. "It's sitting in orbit, right? Fully fueled and waiting?"

"Pre-positioned," Elena confirmed. "Launched on an unmanned cargo mission eighteen months before we arrived. Fueled, checked out, put into a stable parking orbit around Mars. We fly up to it, we dock, we go home. That was the plan."

"Was," Arun repeated quietly.

Elena didn't argue with him. She'd known Arun long enough — not before this mission, but she'd read his files, she knew the way he thought — to understand that when he questioned a word, he was already three steps behind it, looking at all the structural supports and asking which ones were load-bearing and which ones were just decoration.

"Okay," Elena said. "We have work to do. Let's reconvene in forty-eight hours with initial assessments. Until then, keep your heads, keep the systems running, and call me if anything changes. Anything."

They nodded. They dispersed. The galley emptied one by one, leaving Elena alone with the timeline on the wall and the empty white bar at the end that was supposed to be the way home.

---

The power engineering lab was a converted storage module, not much wider than a hallway, lined with equipment that Arun had reorganized three separate times since arrival because the original configuration was, in his assessment, "organized by someone who had never worked in gravity one-third of what God intended." The panels were illuminated by a single overhead strip that hummed at a frequency he'd been meaning to fix for six months.

Imani found him crouched beneath a distribution panel, multimeter clipped to a bus bar, reading voltage in the half-dark.

She didn't announce herself. She just leaned against the door frame and waited. After a moment, he exhaled, disconnected the leads, and slid out from under the panel.

"You came to talk about the briefing," he said.

"I came because I know you, and you're going to sit here with this panel until you either figure out why it hums or forget to eat, and I've decided to save the panel."

He smiled despite himself. "The hum is from a loose filter capacitor on the DC-DC converter. I've been meaning to—"

"Fix it. Yes. You said so six months ago." She stepped into the room and sat on a crate he used as a workbench. "Arun."

He sat down opposite her, elbows on his knees. In the narrow light, he looked older than thirty-four. Everyone did. Mars did that — the lower gravity was supposed to feel freeing, but instead it felt like the whole planet was leaning on you, asking what gave you the right to stand on its surface.

"We need to talk about what rescue actually means," Imani said.

Arun nodded. He had known this was coming. He'd been building towards it in his own head since the briefing, stacking up the facts like blocks, trying to find a configuration that didn't collapse under its own weight.

"Let me walk through it," he said. "You'll correct me where I'm wrong."

"Try me."

"Okay. So Elena showed the timeline. Two years, then home. Simple. Clean. The problem is that the return isn't simple and it sure isn't clean. It never was."

He stood up, walked to the whiteboard that covered one wall, and picked up a marker. The surface was already half-covered with circuit diagrams, and he found a clear patch near the center to begin.

"The ERV is in orbit," he said. "Right now, as we speak, it's circling Mars. That's true. It has fuel, or it should have fuel — I'd want to verify the tank pressure telemetry, but let's assume it's fine. The question is not whether the ERV exists. The question is the chain of things that make the ERV usable."

He drew a circle and wrote *ERV / Mars Orbit*.

"To use the ERV, we need to launch the ascent vehicle from the surface. That's the MAV — the Mars Ascent Vehicle. It's here on the ground, pre-positioned, fueled with methane and oxygen manufactured from local resources. ISRU — in-situ resource utilization. It's been running for years, building up the propellant. That part works. That part is done."

He drew an arrow upward: *MAV: surface → orbit*.

"But the MAV gets us to orbit only. It's not designed for trans-Earth injection. We rendezvous with the ERV, dock, transfer, and then the ERV fires its own engine to send us home. That second burn — the trans-Earth injection burn — requires precise navigation, precise timing, and an engine that has been sitting exposed to cosmic radiation and micrometeorite flux in Mars orbit for at least eighteen months without maintenance."

He drew another arrow: *TEI burn → Earth trajectory*.

"That's piece one," Arun said. "The hardware chain. MAV up to orbit, dock with ERV, ERV burns us home. It was designed to work once, in one specific window, under one specific set of conditions. If anything about those conditions changes, the chain breaks."

Imani was following closely. "What conditions?"

"Launch windows," Arun said. He wrote *26 months* on the board. "Earth and Mars orbit the sun at different speeds, different distances. The planets line up for an efficient Hohmann transfer orbit only once every twenty-six months. That's the golden window. That's when the delta-v — the energy you need — is at its absolute minimum. If you miss the window, you can still go. But you need more fuel, more time, and your consumables were not designed for a longer trip."

He drew two circles around the first one, showing orbits, and marked the alignment point.

"Our planned departure was locked to a specific window. Month twenty-four of the mission, give or take a few weeks for operational flexibility. If we miss that window, the next one is twenty-six months later. That pushes our return out to four-plus years total."

Imani's expression tightened. "We don't have four years of food."

"No. We don't." He added a line to the bottom of the board, wrote *CONSUMABLES: ~620 days*. "So the window matters. But it's not the only thing."

He turned back to the board, and next to the hardware chain, he started drawing a second column. This one was longer, more complex. He wrote *EARTH INFRASTRUCTURE* at the top and underlined it twice.

"Here's the part nobody says out loud at the briefings," he said slowly. "Rescue isn't a single rocket. People picture it that way — you send up a rescue ship, the rescue ship arrives, everyone goes home. It's clean in the movies."

He began writing items below the heading, one by one, ticking them off on his fingers.

"Rescue is a launch vehicle assembly facility on Earth. Those don't just exist. They have supply chains — thousands of suppliers, specialized contractors, rare-earth elements, custom avionics. Rescue is a mission control team, hundreds of people who know our vehicle inside and out, running simulations, preparing procedures. Rescue is political will — a government that has to justify spending billions on six astronauts when it might be facing crises at home. Rescue is an orbital mechanics team that recalculates every burn, every trajectory, every contingency for a mission profile that may no longer match the original plan."

He stepped back from the board. Two columns now faced them. On the left, the hardware: MAV, ERV, TEI burn, orbital rendezvous. On the right, the civilization: manufacturing, personnel, politics, computation, coordination.

"Here's my real concern," Arun said, his voice lower now, almost conversational, the way you talk when what you're saying is too big for volume to carry properly. "Our return was designed as the end of a sequence. The last step. Earth launches us, we go to Mars, we do the science, we come home. The whole chain — manufacturing to mission control to launch to rendezvous to return — was sustained by Earth's industrial and political will over a period of about ten years of planning and building. It was a civilization-scale effort compressed into a mission that, for us, is supposed to just end."

He turned to face her. "The question is whether that civilization is still organized to care about what happens to us."

Imani sat very still. The hum of the DC-DC converter filled the silence between his words.

"We don't know what's happening on Earth," she said finally.

"No. We don't."

"The three days of silence could be a solar storm. Could be equipment failure at the relay satellite. Could be—" She stopped herself.

"Yes," Arun said.

She looked at the whiteboard. Two columns, one neat and finite, the other sprawling and uncertain. The hardware you could assess. You could run the tests, check the telemetry, calculate the margins. The civilization side — that was the ghost in the machinery, the invisible scaffold holding everything up, and if that scaffold was gone, no amount of engineering on this end would matter.

"So what are you saying?" Imani asked, though she already knew. "That we might be here longer than planned?"

"I'm saying that rescue isn't one rocket," Arun said. "Rescue is a whole civilization deciding to keep building one more bridge to reach us. And right now, we can't see whether they're still building."

She absorbed that. She let it sit. The phrase — *a whole civilization deciding to keep building one more bridge* — settled between them like a physical object, heavy and true.

"We need to tell Elena," Imani said.

Arun shook his head. "We will. But not with uncertainty. She asked for numbers. I need to give her numbers. I need to know — concretely — how many suit cycles we have, how the ERV telemetry looks, what the actual consumable count is in every subsystem, not the planned count but the real consumption rate adjusted for actual use. I need to know if the ISRU plant has been making propellant on schedule or if it's been drifting. And I need Imani Okoro to tell me our environmental systems can last."

"Give me a week," Imani said. "I'll run diagnostics on everything from atmospheric scrubbers to water recovery rates, and I'll model it forward, not just at current consumption but at reduced rates, stressed rates, failed-component rates. Everything."

"And the greenhouse modules?" Arun asked. "The biomass yield?"

"I'm already tracking it. The numbers are — they're okay. They're not great, but they're not zero. We're not going to starve next month. But we're not going to feed this crew for three years on it either."

Aron nodded. He capped the marker, set it down, and looked at the whiteboard one more time — the hardware chain and the civilization chain, side by side, two ways of understanding the same impossible distance.

"We'll give Elena what she asked for," he said. "Numbers. Ranges. Worst cases. And she'll decide what to do with the truth."

---

Tomas had been standing outside the power lab for twelve minutes.

He hadn't intended to eavesdrop. He had been walking back from the EVA staging area, where he'd been conducting a hands-on evaluation of the remaining spacesuit inventory, and he had passed the open door of the power lab and heard Arun's voice and stopped because he knew that tone. It was the same tone Arun used during pre-mission training when he was about to explain why something was significantly worse than it appeared in the briefing slides.

Tomas pressed back against the bulkhead wall and listened.

He heard enough.

He wasn't a systems engineer or a mission planner. He was a field geologist who had been hired because he could read Martian rock formations the way some people read poetry and because he could hike for twelve hours in a pressurized suit and come back with samples intact. He understood rocks and terrain and the practical realities of moving through an environment that wanted to kill you in ways that were entirely indifferent to human existence.

But he wasn't stupid.

He heard Arun's voice through the thin door — the careful, measured explanation of the return chain, the MAV, the ERV, the launch windows, the twenty-six-month cycle. He heard Imani say, *We don't have four years of food.* And he heard Arun say the thing that lodged in his chest and stayed: *Rescue is a whole civilization deciding to keep building one more bridge.*

Tomas closed his eyes. He thought about the samples he'd collected outside, sitting in the storage module, labeled and cataloged and waiting to go home with the crew that would put them on a return vehicle and hand them to scientists who would write papers and change textbooks. He thought about the way Earth light looked through the habitat windows at dawn — not blue, exactly, but the color a photograph of Earth would have if someone had described it to you over the phone.

He thought about bridges.

In Sweden, where he'd grown up, there was a bridge called the Öresund Bridge that connected Malmö to Copenhagen. Half bridge, half tunnel, eight kilometers long. He remembered crossing it as a child, pressed against the car window, watching the water below and feeling the impossible reality of human engineering spanning something that was supposed to be unspannable.

*That's what rescue is,* Arun had said. A bridge. Not a vehicle. A structure. Something built from both sides, meeting in the middle, supported by the willingness of people on one end to keep driving pilings and welding beams and paying attention even when the other end was invisible.

Tomas pushed off from the wall and continued walking. He went back to the EVA staging area and sat down next to the row of spacesuits hanging on their racks, six suits in a row, each one inspected and logged and ready for one more walk. He counted the remaining EVA cycles in his head. The numbers were adequate. Not generous, but adequate. For the original mission.

He pulled out his field notebook and began to write down everything he remembered from the conversation he'd overheard. Not because he was supposed to. Not because Elena had assigned him this. But because if they were going to survive whatever came next, every one of them needed to understand what the real situation was, not the briefing-book version.

The notes were rough, in Swedish and English, fragments of sentences and numbers and the bridge metaphor written in bold letters twice because it was important and he needed to feel it on paper. When he was done, he closed the notebook, put it in his jacket, and went to find Chen Wei.

Chen was in the galley, alone, at the table, still carrying the same physical notebook from the briefing. Tomas sat across from him.

"I heard something," Tomas said in English, then in Mandarin when he saw Chen looking up: "我听到了一些事情。"

Chen set his pen down. His face was unreadable, the way it often was — not closed, exactly, but reserved, as if he was always processing information one layer deeper than the level at which he was communicating.

"About comms," Tomas said. "About return."

Chen was quiet for a long moment. Then he reached across the table, opened his own notebook to a page of dense calculations, and turned it to face Tomas.

"You are not the first to look for answers," Chen said. "These are my consumables projections. Not the official numbers. The real numbers, based on actual usage from the past eleven months, not the pre-mission estimates."

Tomas looked down. The spreadsheet was meticulous — daily caloric intake measured against actual consumption, water reclamation efficiency trending downward at a rate that was barely noticeable until you projected it forward six months, spare parts usage rates that were higher than planned because Mars was harsher than anyone had fully anticipated.

"The margin is closing," Chen said quietly. "Not tomorrow. Not next week. But the line goes down, always down."

Mission Planning had discouraged personal items on the grounds of mass and distraction, and Elena, perhaps because she was more disciplined than she'd wanted to be, had complied. The only thing on the wall was a small magnetic strip where she kept a folded printout of the mission timeline — the same one she'd shown in the briefing. The last bar was still white.

She stopped speaking. The recorder hummed quietly, waiting.

Outside her door, the habitat carried on. She could hear the faint vibration of the environmental systems, always on, always running, keeping the air breathable and the temperature survivable. Somewhere, she could hear Tomas moving through the corridor, his footsteps light in the low gravity. Somewhere else, she was pretty sure she heard Imani and Chen talking in low voices, too quiet to make out words.

*We came here on a plan,* she continued. *A good plan. A plan built by hundreds of smart people and tested a thousand times in simulations. The plan assumed that Earth would be doing what Earth had always done: supporting the mission with its full infrastructure, its full attention, its full political and industrial commitment. Two years on Mars. Two years of science. Then come home.*

She picked up the recorder and held it in her palm, watching the green light pulse.

*I need to be honest with myself before I'm honest with anyone else. The communication loss could be temporary. It probably is. Solar activity, relay satellite maintenance, a failed uplink — any one of a dozen mundane things. But the probability of it being temporary is not one hundred percent, and I can't build my crew's survival strategy on probabilities. I need to build it on certainties. And the only certainty I have right now is that the plan is the only plan we have, and plans are made of assumptions.*

She set the recorder down again and leaned back against the bulkhead, closing her eyes.

*Two-year thinking,* she thought. *That's the phrase. Everything we have, everything we are, everything we packed and calibrated and trained for — it's all two-year thinking. Two years of food, two years of parts, two years of suits rotating through their service life. We are a two-year mission sitting on a planet where time is not a concept you can negotiate with.*

Assuming the signal came back.

Earth traffic remained broken.

The optical communications experiment, the one that had been an afterthought during planning, the one nobody counted on — nothing.

"You've been busy," she said.

"I've been honest," he replied.

She read the hardware column. MAV status, ERV telemetry requirements, orbital mechanics calculations, launch window analysis. She turned to him. "You think about this the same way I do."

"I think about it as an engineer," Arun said. "The question is whether the problem is engineering or whether the problem is —" He gestured at the civilization column.

"Whether the problem is that no one is looking back at us," Elena finished for him.

She studied the board a moment longer, then picked up a marker from the tray and added her own notation. Not words. A symbol. She drew a line between the two columns, right at the center, connecting *TEI burn* on the left to *Mission Control* on the right. The line was a bridge of sorts — a dependency. "If we miss the window, the fuel sits in the tanks longer. Methane is stable. The liquid oxygen, less so. So at twenty-six months of additional delay, we'd lose a significant portion of our ascent capability."

"Theoretically. The ISRU plant keeps producing. But its production rate is tuned to build up the required amount and then cycle down. Running it for an extended period means more maintenance, more consumables for the plant itself, more demands on our power grid." He pointed to the power column on the board. "Everything is connected."

"Coming in forty-eight hours. She's running the full suite — atmospheric scrubbing, temperature regulation, water reclamation, waste processing. She'll have numbers."

"And Chen?"

"Chen already has numbers. I saw him in the galley with Tomas. They were looking at caloric projections. I think Chen is further ahead on his analysis than he'll admit during the briefing."

Elena almost smiled. "He's always further ahead than he admits. That's just Chen."

She capped the marker and stepped back from the whiteboard. The two columns and the bridge line between them filled her vision. On one side: machines, physics, chemistry, the things you could measure. On the other: people, decisions, politics, money, the things you couldn't measure from Mars but without which nothing else mattered.

"Some of them won't be ready," Arun said quietly. He was thinking of Tomas. Everyone thought of Tomas when it came to readiness — not because he was fragile, but because he carried things on the inside that he never put on the outside.

"Some of them won't be ready," Elena agreed. "But we're not asking them to be ready. We're asking them to be informed. Being ready comes later."

She turned toward the door. It was time to circulate, to check in with each person individually before the group briefing. That was her method, learned over years of command — talk to people one-on-one first, hear what they're thinking in private, then bring it all together in public so nobody is ambushed by their own worst fears.

But before she left, she stopped in the doorway and looked back at the whiteboard one more time. Two columns. One bridge. A whole civilization, reduced to a question mark.

*Arun,* she said, not turning back. *You said it perfectly. Rescue isn't one rocket.*

"No," he agreed from behind her.

*It's a bridge,* she said. *And right now, we can see our end of it. We just can't see if anyone's still building on the other side.*

*Arun was quiet for a moment. Then: "Then we keep our end maintained."*

Elena nodded to herself. "That's exactly what we do."

*Talos Station, Mars Surface. Mission Day 412. End of Shift Log — Mission AI.*

*Mission AI: "All crew members accounted for. Environmental systems within acceptable thresholds. Water reclamation efficiency: eighty-seven percent. Atmospheric composition: nominal, carbon dioxide scrubbers operating at reduced capacity, recommended filter replacement within fourteen days. Power generation: solar array output at ninety-four percent of seasonal projection, dust accumulation within tolerance, next cleaning cycle scheduled for Mission Day 416. Consumables inventory updated and cross-referenced against all subsystem models. Communications link: no signal from Earth relay network. I am maintaining buffer storage for all outgoing telemetry. I await the signal to transmit. I do not know how long I will wait."*

The AI's voice, when it spoke aloud, was designed to be neutral. Flat. Genderless, accentless, the auditory equivalent of a blank sheet of paper. Mission Planning had calibrated it this way deliberately, based on studies that showed crews performed better when the ship's intelligence didn't simulate personality traits or emotional content.

But if you listened closely enough, if you were the kind of person who had been on Mars for four hundred and twelve days and had nothing but time to develop a relationship with the only constant presence in your life, you could hear something in the AI's final sentence.

Or you could imagine it.

Elena was in her quarters again, the personal recorder still on the table. She hadn't transmitted her private log. She wasn't ready to make it official. But she'd made it, and making it meant that the thought existed in the world, recorded and timestamped and impossible to un-say.

She looked out through the small viewport in the bulkhead — just a circle of reinforced glass, twenty centimeters across, showing a sliver of the Martian surface in the dying light. The sky was the color of rust and dried blood, the same color it had been for four hundred and twelve days, the same color it would be until she looked through a different window on a different vehicle heading home.

Two-year thinking. Everything in this room, in this habitat, in this mission, was designed for two-year thinking.

But survival, she was beginning to understand, required a longer view. It required thinking in terms not of years but of civilizations, not of schedules but of sustained will, not of plans but of the people who made the plans and the people who were still supposed to care about them from the other end of an empty radio channel.

She turned off the main light and sat in the darkness, thinking about bridges and what it meant to stand on one end and wait for the other end to reach back.

---

*End of Chapter 5 — Bridge: They move from uncertainty to math.*
